content: In patients diagnosed with hypertriglyceridemia, dietary management can be implemented either as a standalone intervention or in conjunction with triglyceride-lowering medications. Lifestyle modifications, including dietary adjustments, regular physical activity, smoking cessation, and reduced alcohol consumption, are effective in promoting weight loss. This weight reduction subsequently leads to a mild-to-moderate decrease in triglyceride levels (approximately 22%) and an increase in HDL cholesterol levels (approximately 9%). Dietary Management 1. Increasing the intake of complex carbohydrates, such as dietary fiber, is beneficial. 2. Limiting the consumption of simple carbohydrates, particularly fructose, is crucial. Fructose is present in high amounts in non-diet sodas, fruit juices, and corn syrup, and it can contribute to postprandial hypertriglyceridemia. 3. Reducing the intake of foods high in saturated fats is recommended. 4. Increasing the consumption of monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, such as omega-3 fatty acids found in fatty fish (e.g., sardines, herring, and mackerel), can significantly lower triglyceride levels. When consumed in large quantities (>10 g/day, equivalent to approximately 1 pound of fish by weight) or taken in capsule form, omega-3 fatty acids can reduce triglyceride levels by 40% or more. 5. For patients with triglyceride levels exceeding 1000 mg/dL, dietary fat intake should be restricted to no more than 10% of total caloric intake. This fat restriction aids in weight loss and reduces triglyceride levels, including chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL). However, fat restriction must be approached cautiously: In overweight patients with moderately elevated triglycerides, a very low-fat diet may paradoxically increase triglyceride levels and decrease HDL cholesterol levels. In patients with isolated triglyceride elevation and stable weight, initiating a low-fat diet may lead to further increases in triglyceride levels. In such cases, incorporating monounsaturated or polyunsaturated fats into the diet can lower triglycerides and LDL cholesterol while increasing HDL cholesterol. Physical Activity Current guidelines recommend engaging in regular moderate-intensity physical activity for at least 30 minutes continuously, at least five days per week, ideally every day. Recent studies have shown that cardiovascular exercise is therapeutic in approximately 31% of cases, with the most significant benefit observed in triglyceride levels (43% of participants showed improvement). However, 91% of test subjects did not exhibit reductions in fasting plasma glucose or insulin resistance. For patients unable to perform intensive exercises, weight reduction can still be achieved through dietary modifications and a daily walking routine. Cigarette Smoking Cigarette smoking is a well-established risk factor for premature coronary artery disease and can accelerate cardiovascular risk by approximately 10 years. Smoking cessation is associated with improvements in lipid profiles, despite the potential for weight gain that often accompanies quitting. Alcohol Consumption While some studies suggest that moderate alcohol consumption may reduce the risk of atherosclerotic diseases, it can also increase the risks of hypertension and hemorrhagic stroke.
